title: Market, Credit, Liquidity, Operational and Model Risk
objectives: Define the five major risk categories and give a concrete example of each
Classify a described loss event into the correct risk category
Explain why the same position can carry several risk types simultaneously
Describe how each risk type is typically measured and controlled
motivation: Before any risk can be measured it must be named. Banks organise entire departments around a taxonomy, market risk in one building, operational risk in another, because each type demands different data, models and controls. If you cannot classify a loss event, you cannot choose the right tool to size it, and regulators will hold the wrong capital against it.

blocks.md: Risk is uncertainty that can lead to an adverse outcome. This lesson uses five useful, overlapping categories: market, credit, liquidity, operational and model risk. This is an organising lens, not an exhaustive list of regulatory capital buckets. Classify the mechanism of a loss before choosing its measure or control; concentration, legal and other risks may cross these categories.

rows: Prices and rates moving against you
A \$10m equity book falls 1% in a day: \$100k loss
Owed \$5m on a defaulted loan, recover only 40%: \$3m loss
Not being able to trade or fund quickly at fair value
Hold \$20m of a bond that trades \$2m/day: exit takes days at worsening prices
Position limits vs volume, funding buffers
A fat-finger order buys 1,000,000 shares instead of 100,000
A pricing model uses the wrong volatility: options systematically mispriced

blocks.md: Market risk has the richest toolkit because price data is abundant. A quick sizing: a desk holds \$10m of bonds with modified duration 5. If rates rise by $1\%$ ($100$ basis points), the loss is approximately $5 \times 1\% \times 10{,}000{,}000 = \$500{,}000$. This is a first-order rate-shock approximation, not an exact price change: convexity and nonparallel curve moves can matter.

blocks.text: Credit and liquidity: the asymmetric pair

blocks.md: Credit risk losses are lumpy: most counterparties pay, one defaults and wipes out years of spread income. Expected loss decomposes cleanly:

blocks.caption: Probability of default $\times$ loss given default $\times$ exposure at default
With independent default probability 4% in this toy model, 400 trials have 16 expected defaults. The realised count varies. A default count alone says nothing about severity or correlated defaults.

blocks.md: Risk taxonomies are not academic furniture, they are the table of contents of a risk system. Every category implies a *different measurement machinery*, a different owner, and a different cadence: market risk is measured continuously from positions and prices; credit risk from counterparty exposures and probabilities; operational risk from incident data and process maps; model risk from validation and benchmarking. When a loss happens, the taxonomy tells you which machinery failed, and when a *new* risk appears (crypto custody? an LLM in the pricing path?), the first argument is always "which bucket does this belong in, and does that bucket have machinery?"

Risks interact. Falling prices can increase collateral demands, creating a funding problem; forced selling can then widen spreads and worsen losses. A firm-level scenario therefore crosses categories. For an operational example, suppose a deployment reactivates an obsolete order path and sends unintended orders. The initiating failure is operational even though the resulting position then suffers market risk. A taxonomy helps assign checks and owners, but it cannot prove that one event belongs exclusively to one bucket.

blocks.title: Interview framing: "name the risks in this trade"
blocks.md: Given "buy an illiquid bond, finance it overnight in repo, hedge rates with a future," the expected ladder: market risk (rate moves on the bond) → funding liquidity (repo rolls daily; a spike strands you) → asset liquidity (the bond cannot be sold at mid when you need to) → basis risk between bond and future → counterparty/credit on the repo counterparty. Walking that ladder calmly, one bucket at a time, is precisely the competence the question tests.

Example: PD $= 2\%$, LGD $= 60\%$ (recovery 40%), EAD $= \$5m$: expected loss $= 0.02 \times 0.6 \times 5{,}000{,}000 = \$60{,}000$. Liquidity risk interacts with everything else: a market shock widens spreads and dries depth, so the same position becomes harder to exit exactly when its value is falling, market and liquidity risk compound in crises.

blocks.text: Operational and model risk: the human ones

blocks.md: Operational risk covers rogue trading, failed settlements, cyber incidents and fat fingers, losses from *how* the firm runs, not from markets. Model risk is subtler: your P&L can look perfect while the model is wrong, because the model is also what generates the P&L. The defence is independence: effective challenge needs objective expertise and sufficient independence; validation should use appropriate external evidence, benchmarks and outcomes rather than treating model-generated marks as proof.

blocks.title: One position, several risks
blocks.md: A single corporate bond carries credit risk (issuer default), market risk (spread and rate moves), liquidity risk (thin secondary market) and even model risk (if your credit model misweights recovery). Taxonomy is a lens, not a property of the instrument, classify the *loss mechanism*, not the asset.

blocks.title: Model risk hides in model-driven P&L
blocks.md: If your valuation model marks the book, then 'the model works' is circular reasoning. Ask where an independent, observable price could contradict the model, that is where model risk actually gets discovered, usually at the worst possible time.

guidedExercise.prompt: Classify each event into one of the five categories and justify in one line: (a) A trading algorithm doubles its intended order size due to a unit error in the sizing function. (b) A dealer fails to deliver securities it sold. (c) An equity hedge loses money because correlations used to build it spiked in a crash. (d) The firm's risk report understates exposure because its VaR model ignores a volatility regime change.
hints: Ask: what failed, a price, a counterparty, tradability, a process, or a model?
(a) is about how the firm executed, not about any market move.
Check the units and name the initiating loss mechanism; add a second category when your explanation depends on an interaction.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) Operational risk, a process/system error (sizing bug). (b) Credit/counterparty risk, the counterparty failed to perform on its obligation. (c) Market risk, price/correlation movement against the book as the initiating event; there may also be model risk if the hedge relied on an unjustified constant-correlation assumption. (d) Model risk, the model's assumptions failed; the loss mechanism is an incorrect model, though the realised P&L hit arrives through market moves.
guidedExercise.successCheck: You identify the initiating mechanism for all four events and explain why market and model risk may coexist in the correlation example.

independentExercise.prompt: Compute the expected credit loss and the 50-basis-point rate-shock loss, then classify the residual exposures: A bank has lent \$8m to a firm with PD 3% and LGD 50%. Separately it holds \$12m of bonds with modified duration 4. (a) Expected credit loss on the loan. (b) Approximate loss if rates rise 50 basis points. (c) If the bonds are illiquid (daily volume \$1m), what additional risk category applies to exiting the position?
hints: Duration loss $\approx$ duration $\times$ rate move $\times$ notional; 50bp $= 0.5\%$.
Check the units and name the initiating loss mechanism; add a second category when your explanation depends on an interaction.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $0.03 \times 0.5 \times 8{,}000{,}000 = \$120{,}000$. (b) $4 \times 0.005 \times 12{,}000{,}000 = \$240{,}000$ (market risk). (c) Liquidity risk: exiting \$12m into a \$1m/day market takes many days at widening prices, an inventory/liquidity exposure on top of the market-risk mark.
independentExercise.successCheck: Expected loss is 120,000 dollars and the first-order 50bp rate-shock loss is 240,000 dollars; you separately identify exit liquidity risk and state the approximation.

commonMistakes: Classifying by instrument rather than by loss mechanism, the same bond can carry four risk types.
Treating liquidity risk as merely 'slow trading', it also means funding risk: inability to meet obligations at fair cost.
Assuming model risk is caught by back-testing the P&L when the P&L is model-generated; independent validation is required.
Confusing expected loss (a priced cost, provisioned) with unexpected loss (the risk around it, held as capital).
realWorldApplication: A risk taxonomy helps firms organise controls, incident reporting and scenario analysis. Actual regulatory categories, reporting processes and committee schedules depend on jurisdiction, institution and activity; this five-category teaching lens does not prescribe them.
quantFinanceApplication: Quant developers build the classification into their risk systems: every position carries market-risk sensitivities, counterparty exposures, liquidity scores and model-version tags, so a single trade feeds four different risk dashboards.
summary: Five categories: market (prices), credit (counterparty default), liquidity (tradability/funding), operational (people/processes/systems), model (your own models).
Expected credit loss $= \text{PD} \times \text{LGD} \times \text{EAD}$; market-risk sizing starts as sensitivity $\times$ shock.
Liquidity risk compounds with market risk in crises: spreads widen and depth disappears when prices fall.
Classify by loss mechanism, not by instrument, and validate models independently of those who build them.

quiz.prompt: Which category-to-mechanism pairings match the five-category lens in this lesson?
options: Market: adverse movements in prices or rates
Credit: a borrower or counterparty failing to pay
Liquidity: inability to fund or exit at acceptable cost
Operational: failures of processes, people or systems
Model: incorrect assumptions, implementation or use of a model
Credit: any price movement in an exchange-traded asset
Liquidity: a software deployment that sends unintended orders
quiz.explanation: The first five pairings identify the mechanisms, not just the instrument involved. A price move alone is market risk rather than a credit default. An unintended order caused by deployment is an operational failure, although the resulting position can also create market and liquidity exposure.

quiz.prompt: PD = 2%, LGD = 60%, EAD = \$5m. Expected credit loss in dollars?
quiz.explanation: Expected loss is probability of default times loss given default times exposure: 0.02 times 0.60 times 5,000,000 gives 60,000 dollars. Using the 40% recovery rate as LGD would understate loss: LGD is one minus recovery.

quiz.prompt: A \$10m bond position has modified duration 5. Rates rise 100bp. Approximate loss in dollars?
quiz.explanation: Modified duration gives an approximate fractional price change of minus duration times the yield change. Five times 0.01 times 10 million gives a 500,000-dollar loss. The sign is a fall in price for a rise in yield; convexity is omitted in this first-order estimate.

quiz.prompt: Which statements correctly describe model risk?
options: It can exist even while reported P&L looks healthy
It is eliminated once a model passes back-testing
Independent validation is a standard control
It only affects pricing desks, never risk reporting
quiz.explanation: Model-generated P&L cannot validate its own generator, and risk reports inherit model risk too. Passing one back-test is evidence, not elimination.

quiz.prompt: Explain why one illiquid corporate bond can carry credit, market and liquidity risk simultaneously.
quiz.modelAnswer: The issuer can default, yields or spreads can move against the holder, and thin trading depth can make a sale costly or slow. These are separate loss mechanisms on the same position.
quiz.explanation: The instrument does not determine a single risk label. Default concerns promised payments, market risk concerns repricing, and liquidity concerns the cost or timing of funding or sale. A defaulted or falling bond may also become harder to trade, so the mechanisms can interact.

quiz.prompt: A fund cannot meet a redemption because its assets cannot be sold fast enough at fair value. This is fundamentally:
quiz.explanation: The loss mechanism is inability to convert assets to cash quickly at fair value, liquidity risk (specifically funding/market liquidity interacting with redemption terms).

flashcards.back: Market, credit, liquidity, operational, model, classified by loss mechanism, not by instrument.
$EL = PD \times LGD \times EAD$ - probability of default times loss given default times exposure at default.
$\Delta P \approx -D \times \Delta y \times V$; e.g. duration 5, +100bp on \$10m $\Rightarrow$ \$500k loss.

Model marks cannot validate themselves. Objective challenge uses conceptual review, suitable benchmarks, external evidence and outcomes to detect errors or misuse. No single back-test eliminates model risk.
